description: One self-describing JSON becomes one frame-perfect video. A deterministic motion-graphics engine for people and coding agents: write a scene as data, render an mp4, get the same bytes every time.
rules: A film is ONE self-describing JSON with "module": "scene". There is exactly one module and there are no templates: compose every video from primitives rather than copying a structure.
renderFrame(n) is pure in n. A frame may never depend on wall-clock time, randomness without a seed, or any state outside the scene. This is the load-bearing invariant of the whole engine.
Read films/scene/schema.json for the contract before writing a scene. It is the source of truth for every field.
A scene needs only five keys to exist: module, theme, duration, layers and bg. Everything else is optional.
Author a boundary through transitions[] only. cuts, stings and seams are its lowered internal form and the validator refuses them written directly.

Reference things by name rather than by number where the engine allows it. A cursor aims at a layer with snapTo, a layer sits at a named place with pin, text takes a role with size: "headline", and a time can be written against another layer, as start: "someLayerId+0.4". A number is right when it is a decision; a reference is right when it is a relationship.
Never write an em dash (U+2014) in on-screen text. The validator rejects it.
Prefer a camera move and a boundary treatment over a stack of layers that appear and disappear. A film with neither reads as a slideshow.
camera: hold is a real declaration meaning the camera is locked off. It is not an alias of driftHold, which breathes.
Sound is derived, not hand-placed: audio.tactile reads the timeline you already wrote and a cue is derived at every cut and seam. Pin a hand-placed cue to an event rather than to a clock.
Run make author-check D=<file> before shipping a scene, then make judge after rendering. The judge is the only step that sees the output.
